name: 《Jae-Eun Choi : Promise (Where Being Be)》
summary: A solo exhibition by Jae-Eun Choi that connects the timeline from the origins of humanity to ecological crisis, calling attention to human responsibility for the destruction of nature and life and to
description_html: 《Promise (Where Being Be)》 presents the concept of mutual coexistence beyond linguistic meaning, recalling the interconnected solidarity of nature that has traversed time and space long before civilization. Just as the origins of the words promise and bind are intertwined, beings have long been entangled like threads and have existed together through vast stretches of time. The exhibition consists of five subthemes Lucy, Warning Bell, Microcosm, Subtle Name, and Natural State Beyond Boundaries, along with an archive that surveys the artist’s major body of work. By summoning the long timeline shared by early humans and ourselves, the exhibition reveals the responsibility humanity must bear for the destruction of nature and life, evoking the possibility of coexistence through bleached coral, life in the Demilitarized Zone, and disappearing wildflowers, and leading toward the path of ecological solidarity proposed by the artist. Amid rapidly changing global environments, 《Jae-Eun Choi : Promise (Where Being Be)》 asks what kind of life we should aspire to.

name: 《Electric Shock》
summary: An exhibition that traces the sharp relationship between technology and the environment unfolding today through the single circuit of electricity, reexamining the role of art while exploring methods o
description_html: 《Electric Shock》 is a report on electricity. Electricity, defined as the totality of energy generated through electrons, is a key resource that operates modern society. From household appliances to digital consumption, advanced production lines, and logistics systems, it is difficult to imagine life without electricity. The recent commercialization of artificial intelligence and the expansion of big tech companies have exponentially increased power consumption. Securing and supplying electricity in a stable manner has become a critical issue in rapidly adopting advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence, beginning to determine the competitiveness of nations and corporations. The era of electrical hegemony has arrived, and alongside endless desires for technological advancement, various efforts to develop power within finite resources are underway. Electricity is no longer merely an energy source that enriches daily life but has become an essential weapon that determines survival. This urgency has led to indiscriminate development, turning even efforts for carbon neutrality into romantic promises seen as delaying technological progress. Reflective movements that once called for sustainable coexistence such as posthumanism and the Anthropocene are fading into history already written over the immediate electric war unfolding before us. Electric Shock reveals and traces the sharp relationship between technology and the environment occurring today through a single circuit called electricity.

summary: An exhibition introducing creative worlds based on artist research constructed through original approaches that cross multiple academic and technological fields.

This exhibition was planned to reexamine the academic, artistic, and social value of research conducted by artists. The two artists’ explorations of human constructed systems of knowledge and time intersect with studies of natural orders such as vegetation zones and flowering rhythms and are realized through art. This exhibition, which presents different research based artistic practices addressing the relationship between humans and non humans, aims to step away from human centered global thinking and to awaken a planetary sensibility that imagines possibilities of coexistence among the diverse beings that make up the Earth.

name: Munassi 《The Season We Fade Away》
summary: A journey that follows the flow of emotions
description_html:
Space K Seoul is pleased to present The Season We Fade Away, a solo exhibition by Moonassi (b. 1980). Rooted in the traditions of Korean painting, the artist has long explored the mind, human relationships, and the subtle inner currents that flow between them. In this exhibition, his paintings serve as both a journey following the flow of emotions and a site for quiet contemplation of the self.

For Moonassi, each stroke that remains on paper resembles a ripple spreading across the surface of the mind—like a tremor that gently disturbs still water. Just as the faintest vibration expands into waves, the movements of the inner self—elusive and resistant to words—slowly take shape on the picture plane.

The Season We Fade Away reflects on how emotions are born from and fade within relationships. Emotions are awakened and stirred by encounters with others. Like waves on the water, relationships and emotions seep into one another, exchanging light. The artist captures these moments of delicate balance: from figures facing one another, to sharing a gaze toward a single point, to pausing for a breath before a face reflected on the water’s surface.

Moonassi does not suppress or define emotions. Instead, he chooses to let them be. This attitude of acceptance becomes a way of seeing the self reflected through others, leading to a quiet observation of one's own being amidst these fluctuations.

As suggested by the characters in his name—"Mu (無: non-)" and "Na (我: self)"— his work traverses the boundaries between fullness and emptiness, the self and the other, peering into the space that lies between. In his compositions where the traditional ink meets modern sensibility, emotions do not simply disappear. Rather, they linger, changing form, only to resurface when the time is right.

The Season We Fade Away is an exhibition that reflects our own faces on the surface of the water where emotion and relationship intersect. Viewers are invited to accept emotions as they are and, in passing through the tremors of relationships, encounter a quiet moment of return to the self.

description_html: The National Museum of Korea presents the special exhibition <Our Yi Sun sin>, commemorating the four hundred eightieth anniversary of the birth of Admiral Yi Sun sin and the eightieth anniversary of Liberation. Centered on records left by Yi Sun sin himself, this exhibition sheds light on his inner thoughts and emotions beyond his role as a war hero, as well as on how he became a symbol shaped by later generations. description_html:
Another story of records at the Seoul Metropolitan Archives

The Seoul Metropolitan Archives presents the exhibition A City’s Boarding Log, introducing the journey of Seoul’s transportation. The exhibition traces the city’s growth from the aftermath of the Korean War to the 1980s, as it built the foundations of its transportation system through archival materials. It showcases more than 120 records owned by the Seoul Metropolitan Archives, as well as donated materials from an engineer involved in the construction of the subway, vividly conveying the atmosphere of that era. In addition, a new permanent space has been created by relocating and reconstructing the exhibition contents of the Seoul Archives and Culture Center on the third floor of the Seoul Metropolitan Library, allowing visitors to explore Seoul from multiple perspectives. Follow the traces of time along the roads of Seoul and reflect on the paths we have taken and those that lie ahead.

name: JEJU HAENYEO : DISAPPEARING WORLDS
summary: An exhibition that reinterprets the ecological and social significance of the Haenyeo culture through experimental works created by artists in collaboration with Haenyeo communities in Jeju.
description_html:
In the summer of 2025, five artists traveled to Jeju. They shared meals with the Haenyeo, sat together at the bulteok, exchanged stories, and observed the tools, discipline, and bodily memories of time. Thus, this exhibition began from two weeks of shared experiences with the Haenyeo. Céline Park examines the hierarchy and silence embedded within the Haenyeo community, Kim Yi-hwa explores the survival of 'nomadic Haenyeo' in the face of climate change, and Moon Su-hyuk critiques how tradition is consumed as a language of capital. Son Ji-min reconsiders the labor of Haenyeo through the lens of femininity and care, while Choi Mi-jin investigates the transmission of knowledge through oral narratives and relationships.

description_html: This opening exhibition of The Prima Art Center unveils for the first time 487 small ceramic pieces collected by the late Lee Woobok, founder of Daewoo Group and a key contributor to Korea’s industrial and economic development. Alongside his corporate career, he deeply appreciated the beauty of Korean art and ceramics and dedicated himself to preserving cultural heritage. He was particularly captivated by the serene and generous beauty of Joseon white porcelain and blue-and-white porcelain, collecting numerous small ceramic works over many years with great care. The exhibition title Sojunghyundae (小中顯大) means “Greatness revealed within smallness.” The 487 artifacts on display include 103 Goryeo celadon pieces, 3 Joseon buncheong ware pieces, and 381 Joseon white porcelain pieces.

name: Play : Crying While Eating Garlic
summary: A story for those who, despite being worn out by constant clashes, eventually find themselves facing one another again.
description_html: Crying While Eating Garlic is a play themed around “the fatigue of coexistence and relationships,” reinterpreting the “Transformation of the Bear and the Tiger into Humans” from the Dangun myth in a contemporary context. The work begins with the question of why the tiger failed to endure “one hundred days in the cave eating only mugwort and garlic.” The play imagines that the reason was the difficulty of coexisting with the bear, and from this perspective, it explores the exhaustion, failures, and subtle efforts of coexistence that we encounter today. The performance is composed not as a single narrative but as a collage of short, repeated scenes.
description_text: Crying While Eating Garlic is a play themed around “the fatigue of coexistence and relationships,” reinterpreting the “Transformation of the Bear and the Tiger into Humans” from the Dangun myth in a contemporary context. The work begins with the question of why the tiger failed to endure “one hundred days in the cave eating only mugwort and garlic.” The play imagines that the reason was the difficulty of coexisting with the bear, and from this perspective, it explores the exhaustion, failures, and subtle efforts of coexistence that we encounter today. The performance is composed not as a single narrative but as a collage of short, repeated scenes.

name: Cheonggyecheon Museum, Twenty
summary: The Cheonggyecheon Museum presents an exhibition celebrating its twentieth anniversary.
description_html:
The year 2025 marks both the twentieth anniversary of the completion of the Cheonggyecheon restoration and the twentieth anniversary of the opening of the Cheonggyecheon Museum. The Cheonggyecheon Museum began as an exhibition hall to promote the Cheonggyecheon Restoration Project. Ten years after its opening, it was remodeled into a professional museum that comprehensively highlights the history of Cheonggyecheon. Since then, it has actively presented exhibitions, education, research, and cultural events that help citizens better understand Seoul through the history of Cheonggyecheon and its riverside.

This exhibition looks into what the past twenty years of the museum have been filled with through the “Room of a Twenty-Year-Old Youth.” In addition, it provides an opportunity to think about what new horizons Cheonggyecheon, as a historical and cultural content that remembers Seoul, can open in the future.
description_text: The year 2025 marks both the twentieth anniversary of the completion of the Cheonggyecheon restoration and the twentieth anniversary of the opening of the Cheonggyecheon Museum. The Cheonggyecheon Museum began as an exhibition hall to promote the Cheonggyecheon Restoration Project. Ten years after its opening, it was remodeled into a professional museum that comprehensively highlights the history of Cheonggyecheon. Since then, it has actively presented exhibitions, education, research, and cultural events that help citizens better understand Seoul through the history of Cheonggyecheon and its riverside. This exhibition looks into what the past twenty years of the museum have been filled with through the “Room of a Twenty-Year-Old Youth.” In addition, it provides an opportunity to think about what new horizons Cheonggyecheon, as a historical and cultural content that remembers Seoul, can open in the future.

name: The Exhibition 《I Will Come to Like》
summary: The Exhibition I Will Come to Like is held at the Superior Gallery until November 6, 2025
description_html:
Superior Gallery presents a three-artist exhibition The Exhibition 《I Will Come to Like》 by Oksuk, Phonormal, and Frida Ok in October 2025. The three participating artists, who work on both illustration shared in digital environments and original paintings, reconstruct moments of daily life into memories and show a wide range of diversity in works through their respective colors and distinctive expressions.

Oksuk calmly yet vividly depicts scenes of rest and travel discovered in urban daily life, expanding into “emotional landscapes” that record brief moments of rest within a busy life. Phonormal humorously expresses daily life and inner emotions, and through playful color contrasts and composition, completes scenes in which remembered thoughts and new imagery are naturally combined. Frida Ok portrays stories of elderly couples and natural landscapes with warm sentiments, visually conveying the warmth and accumulated time of life through repetitive brushstrokes and the dense flower paths in which the elderly couples appear.

This exhibition aims to deliver visual pleasure and empathy through the works of the three artists and to provide a place where viewers can encounter “scenes they will come to like” within their own memories and emotions. The Exhibition 《I Will Come to Like》 runs until November 6, 2025.
description_text: Superior Gallery presents a three-artist exhibition The Exhibition 《I Will Come to Like》 by Oksuk, Phonormal, and Frida Ok in October 2025. The three participating artists, who work on both illustration shared in digital environments and original paintings, reconstruct moments of daily life into memories and show a wide range of diversity in works through their respective colors and distinctive expressions. Oksuk calmly yet vividly depicts scenes of rest and travel discovered in urban daily life, expanding into “emotional landscapes” that record brief moments of rest within a busy life. Phonormal humorously expresses daily life and inner emotions, and through playful color contrasts and composition, completes scenes in which remembered thoughts and new imagery are naturally combined. Frida Ok portrays stories of elderly couples and natural landscapes with warm sentiments, visually conveying the warmth and accumulated time of life through repetitive brushstrokes and the dense flower paths in which the elderly couples appear. This exhibition aims to deliver visual pleasure and empathy through the works of the three artists and to provide a place where viewers can encounter “scenes they will come to like” within their own memories and emotions. The Exhibition 《I Will Come to Like》 runs until November 6, 2025.

name: Dobong  Kim Sun-young : Solo Exhibition 「Here, Standing on the Star」
summary: The solo exhibition “Here, Standing on a Star” by Kim Sun-young Dobong presents experimental reconstructions of ancient and modern scripts, including oracle bone script and Hangul, within the context
description_html:
Stars are not abstract symbols in the distant sky, they are the very spot where I stand, breathing and living in the present moment. The small tremors and deep immersion we experience in everyday life create a resonance of consciousness, within which a universe, a world, emerges. This exhibition is a condensation of moments deepened and contemplated in prolonged silence and stillness.


Time spent alone, detached from relationships, reflects the paths I have walked and the traces of pauses I have taken, while simultaneously serving as a gateway to another world. Within the context of traditional calligraphy, I evoke the primal forms and energies of ancient scripts, especially oracle bone characters, and reconstruct them with Hangul’s formal possibilities through a contemporary sensibility. The characters go beyond mere tools for communication; they manifest as traces of existence and as visual sculptural forms. Letters that breathe like living hearts engrave a pulse into each stroke, leaving trajectories that pierce through time.


“Here, Standing on a Star” does not refer to any particular star. It is the “here” where I stand, the moments of now. The characters that bloom in this space transcend personal records and explore how humans perceive and sense the world. I hope this exhibition becomes, for visitors, another star and a pathway to their inner selves. Along this journey, I envision embracing even severed relationships without fear, and standing as a radiant being in one’s own right.

name: Unprecedented Great Flood: The 1925 Eulchuk Year
summary: An exhibition reflecting on this historic disaster on the 100th anniversary of the Great Flood of the Eulchuk Year, with the hope of encouraging collective discussion on future climate change prepared
description_html:
In the summer of 1925, the Han River flood claimed numerous lives and destroyed houses and buildings. The city of Gyeongseong was left isolated with electricity and transportation cut off, and farmlands surrounding the city that sustained its residents were washed away or turned into sand fields. The flood even changed the course of the Han River and erased entire villages. Known as the “Great Flood of the Eulchuk Year,” this disaster had both direct and indirect significant impacts on Seoul. Later, when flood control facilities were installed on the Han River, the flood served as the benchmark, and flood control became a major issue in urban planning.


A century later, as continuous flood control efforts have led to floods fading from public memory, the climate crisis has struck. Faced with extreme downpours that have become part of daily life, we are once again reminded of the severity of great floods. On the centennial of the Eulchuk Year Great Flood, this exhibition revisits this historic disaster, serving as an opportunity to collectively consider measures for future climate change preparedness.
description_text: In the summer of 1925, the Han River flood claimed numerous lives and destroyed houses and buildings. The city of Gyeongseong was left isolated with electricity and transportation cut off, and farmlands surrounding the city that sustained its residents were washed away or turned into sand fields. The flood even changed the course of the Han River and erased entire villages. Known as the “Great Flood of the Eulchuk Year,” this disaster had both direct and indirect significant impacts on Seoul. Later, when flood control facilities were installed on the Han River, the flood served as the benchmark, and flood control became a major issue in urban planning. A century later, as continuous flood control efforts have led to floods fading from public memory, the climate crisis has struck. Faced with extreme downpours that have become part of daily life, we are once again reminded of the severity of great floods. On the centennial of the Eulchuk Year Great Flood, this exhibition revisits this historic disaster, serving as an opportunity to collectively consider measures for future climate change preparedness.

description_html: For the artists, working evokes emotions similar to childbirth. The time of anguish and the energy condensed within that time culminate in a moment comparable to the birth of life. Choi Seung-yoon’s abstract works, which serve as the background of the exhibition, reveal the fundamental energy inherent in humanity without reservation. Behind this force lies the artist’s effort to capture on canvas countless emotions that cannot be explained one by one. The fine-brush paintings of artist Cho Jung-eun, who pays attention to vanishing things with affection, are added to the canvas, combining emotion with emotion. This exhibition thus contains narratives of anticipation and joy, as well as responsibility and fear.
description_text: For the artists, working evokes emotions similar to childbirth. The time of anguish and the energy condensed within that time culminate in a moment comparable to the birth of life. name: Hongik University Museum Special Exhibition 《After White 1975–1995》
summary: An exhibition revisiting the writings of critic Lee Il to trace the history of Korean contemporary art through the flow of criticism.
description_html: In 2025, the Hongik University Museum presents the special exhibition After White 1975–1995. This exhibition re-examines the critic Lee Il’s essay White Thinks, which laid the foundations for the aesthetics of Korean monochrome painting (Dansaekhwa), retracing the trajectory of his thought and practice, which deeply influenced the formation and development of Korean contemporary art. From the museum’s collection, visitors will encounter the flow of Korean contemporary art beginning with monochrome painting and the color white, viewed within the context of art criticism. The exhibition provides an opportunity to experience how art and criticism interacted to shape the flow of Korean contemporary art and to newly encounter the influence criticism exerted in Korean art history. It is hoped that this exhibition will re-examine the meaning of criticism within the history of Korean contemporary art and offer an occasion to reflect anew on contemporary art discourse today.
description_text: In 2025, the Hongik University Museum presents the special exhibition After White 1975–1995. This exhibition re-examines the critic Lee Il’s essay White Thinks, which laid the foundations for the aesthetics of Korean monochrome painting (Dansaekhwa), retracing the trajectory of his thought and practice, which deeply influenced the formation and development of Korean contemporary art. From the museum’s collection, visitors will encounter the flow of Korean contemporary art beginning with monochrome painting and the color white, viewed within the context of art criticism. The exhibition provides an opportunity to experience how art and criticism interacted to shape the flow of Korean contemporary art and to newly encounter the influence criticism exerted in Korean art history. It is hoped that this exhibition will re-examine the meaning of criticism within the history of Korean contemporary art and offer an occasion to reflect anew on contemporary art discourse today.

name: The Day of Our Liberation
summary: Exhibition of historical and photographic records of Liberation Day, alongside literature, music, films, and other popular culture materials
description_html:
To commemorate the 80th anniversary of Korea’s Liberation, the special exhibition 'The Day of Our Liberation' is being held. The exhibition is composed of three parts: Part 1 'Records of Liberation Day', Part 2 'Memories of Liberation Day', and Part 3 'Recollections of Liberation Day'. It highlights the Liberation Day commemorative ceremonies and related events, shedding light on how citizens have remembered Liberation Day and the changes in the spirit of the times. In addition, literature, film, music, and other popular culture materials related to Liberation Day are on display, allowing visitors to understand the broader social context of the era.


The exhibition focuses particularly on Liberation Day commemorative ceremonies held after independence, showing how citizens commemorated the event and how the zeitgeist evolved. A highlight of the exhibition is the first public display of a diary donated by a former schoolteacher, covering daily life from June 3 to November 20, 1945. The diary holds special significance as it was written in Japanese before liberation and switched to Korean after news of independence was received.


Through 'The Day of Our Liberation', visitors are invited to reflect on the sacrifices of independence activists and share in the meaning of liberation.

name: The Boundary Unmade: The Destruction of the Seoul City Wall
summary: An exhibition on the demolition of Hanyangdoseong by Japan and the transformation of Seoul into a colonial city
description_html:
In the second half of 2025, the Hanyangdoseong Museum opens its special exhibition Demolition of Hanyangdoseong, Breaking the Boundaries of Hanyang.


King Taejo Yi Seong-gye, founder of the Joseon dynasty, established palaces, the Jongmyo Shrine, and the Sajik Altar in Hanyang based on Confucian ideals, and in 1396 began construction of Hanyangdoseong to defend the capital. The city wall functioned as both a physical boundary separating the capital from the provinces and a symbol of royal authority. After Japan’s victory in the Russo-Japanese War, it began interfering in the Korean Empire, establishing the Wall Disposal Committee in 1907 to commence the full-scale demolition of Hanyangdoseong. Under the pretext of modernization and urban development, gates and walls were destroyed, replaced with colonial government facilities and residential areas.


To mark the 80th anniversary of Liberation, this exhibition presents the process of the demolition of Hanyangdoseong by Japan and the transformation of Seoul into a colonial city, using a wide range of historical materials.

name: SeMA Public Space Project 《The Dance That Crosses Forever》
summary: An installation exhibition that breathes fresh vitality into linear spaces, embodying cycles and balances where center and end, inside and outside, continuously shift.
description_html:
The Seoul Museum of Art presents its 2025 Public Space Project featuring world-renowned artist Ernesto Neto, who has broadened the horizon of contemporary sculpture. His new work Ba Ka Ba, The Dance That Crosses Forever is a large-scale installation traversing the lobby and open areas of the Seosomun Main Building. The work is crafted by crocheting industrial cotton fabrics in brown, reminiscent of tree trunks and night, and in pink, symbolizing flowers and day, filled with locally sourced guava leaves and tea tree leaves.

summary: Kolon’s cultural and artistic sharing space, Space K Seoul, presents the solo exhibition 《Deep Diver》 by Bae Yun Hwan (b. 1983).
description_html:

Bae Yun Hwan is an artist who begins with personal experiences and expands his vision to global issues. In his creative process, he unravels not only individual anguish but also the disintegration of communities and the signs of the times such as disasters and wars, expressed through his own allegorical techniques, thereby leading contemporary painting. This exhibition unfolds his narratives more broadly and deeply through works across various genres, including painting, drawing, installation, and video.

name: UAUS 14th Pavilion Exhibition  Ask Nature : Biomimicry
summary: An exhibition exploring the possibilities of sustainable architecture, created by students from 26 architecture departments across Korea
description_html:
'Ask Nature: Biomimicry' is an exhibition centered on architectural wisdom inspired by nature. Students from 26 universities nationwide gather to explore the potential of sustainable architecture through architectural experiments that imitate natural forms, behaviors, and systems.

Moreover, students take full initiative in every stage, from design to production, construction, and dismantling, making the exhibition a laboratory for directly experiencing and sharing the interconnections between architecture and nature, city and environment.

summary: Seoul Arts Center is delighted to present One Step at a Time: Heehwan Seo, a Master of Hangul Calligraphy, an exhibition highlighting the life and art of Pyeongbo Heehwan Seo. Held in commemoration of
description_html:
Seoul Arts Center is delighted to present One Step at a Time: Heehwan Seo, a Master of Hangul Calligraphy, an exhibition highlighting the life and art of Pyeongbo Heehwan Seo. Held in commemoration of the 30th anniversary of Seo’s passing, this large-scale retrospective provides a comprehensive overview of Seo’s extensive oeuvre, spanning works from his early years to his later life.


Seo, also known by his art name “Pyeongbo [one step at a time],” was a representative Hangul calligrapher of 20th-century Korea. In 1968, his presentation won the Presidential Award at the 17th National Art Exhibition of Korea, marking the first time a work of calligraphy received this particular honor. Until his death at the age of 61 in 1995, Seo devoted his entire life to exploring Hangul’s calligraphic potential. This incomparable artistic achievement cements his status as an indispensable figure in the history of Korean calligraphy. 


This exhibition was designed to trace Seo’s journey in achieving the feat of Hangul calligraphy being accepted as an art form. Establishing Hangul calligraphy as an art form — and more importantly, as a calligraphical art — was his lifelong goal, and his perseverance eventually realized this dream. Seo once said, “A turtle in a lake waits a thousand years for its turn to perch atop a lotus leaf,” and his 61-year journey was, indeed, true to his art name, Pyeongbo — one step at a time — in both art and life, advancing step by step without rushing or resting. We hope this exhibition offers visitors an opportunity to deepen their understanding of Seo’s life and art and to keep his memory alive.

In 1968, his presentation won the Presidential Award at the 17th National Art Exhibition of Korea, marking the first time a work of calligraphy received this particular honor. Until his death at the age of 61 in 1995, Seo devoted his entire life to exploring Hangul’s calligraphic potential. This incomparable artistic achievement cements his status as an indispensable figure in the history of Korean calligraphy. This exhibition was designed to trace Seo’s journey in achieving the feat of Hangul calligraphy being accepted as an art form. name: The 13th Seoul Mediacity Biennale: Spell – The Art of the Soul
summary: A large-scale exhibition exploring the convergence of art and spiritual experience.
description_html: The 13th edition of the Seoul Mediacity Biennale, titled 'Spell – The Art of the Soul', will take place from August 26 to November 23, 2025, at the Seoul Museum of Art and various venues throughout the city. This biennale features newly commissioned works, recreations, and existing pieces by artists from around the world, drawing inspiration from the occult, mysticism, and spiritual traditions. It aims to offer the biennale as an “alternative technology” that counters the accelerating, rationalist logic of capitalist modernity and the political and intellectual structures that shape our lived experiences. As a “biennale that proposes mediumistic experience,” the exhibition explores the long-standing human desire to connect with worlds beyond conscious life and examines how communication with the spiritual realm has transformed the language and methods of artistic creation.
description_text: The 13th edition of the Seoul Mediacity Biennale, titled 'Spell – The Art of the Soul', will take place from August 26 to November 23, 2025, at the Seoul Museum of Art and various venues throughout the city. name: Looking at the Calm Light and the Blue Sky
summary: A two-person exhibition by artists Yoon Eui-jin and Lee Chae-il, inviting viewers to reflect on the present and face the possibilities of tomorrow.

name: YMCA Seoul : A Civic History Shaped by Youth
summary: An exhibition showcasing over 120 years of Seoul YMCA’s legacy, offering insight into its rich history of educational, civic, and athletic contributions throughout modern and contemporary times.
description_html: Every year, the Gongpyeong Historic Sites Museum (26, Ujeongguk-ro, Jongno-gu) hosts a special exhibition that highlights the history and significance of the Jongno area. This year marks the museum’s seventh special exhibition, spotlighting the story of YMCA Seoul, which began in the heart of Jongno. The exhibition traces the YMCA’s 120-year journey, offering an in-depth look at its role in Korea’s modern history, particularly in education, civil society, and sports.  Part 1 covers the founding of the YMCA, the construction of its headquarters, and its involvement in nationalist movements during the Japanese occupation period. Part 2 focuses on post-liberation civic movements, while Part 3 presents the introduction and development of everyday sports in modern Korea through photographs, blueprints, publications, and various other materials.
description_text: Every year, the Gongpyeong Historic Sites Museum (26, Ujeongguk-ro, Jongno-gu) hosts a special exhibition that highlights the history and significance of the Jongno area. This year marks the museum’s seventh special exhibition, spotlighting the story of YMCA Seoul, which began in the heart of Jongno. The exhibition traces the YMCA’s 120-year journey, offering an in-depth look at its role in Korea’s modern history, particularly in education, civil society, and sports. Part 1 covers the founding of the YMCA, the construction of its headquarters, and its involvement in nationalist movements during the Japanese occupation period. Part 2 focuses on post-liberation civic movements, while Part 3 presents the introduction and development of everyday sports in modern Korea through photographs, blueprints, publications, and various other materials.

summary:
A new aesthetic trajectory connecting the boundaries between Korean tradition and contemporary art, emerging as a philosophy of sensation
Featuring about 250 works by Korean traditional, modern/
description_html:
《1st Hanbyeol Art Fair – Yeoyeo Nature 如如自然》, a new sensory venue that fuses Korea's unique aesthetics with contemporary artistic philosophy, will be held from Saturday, July 5 to Saturday, August 16 at K Auction Exhibition Hall in Buam-dong, Seoul. 《Hanbyeol Art Fair》 is an exhibition co-hosted by Arterati and K Auction, exploring how art leaves rhythms of sensation and textures of existence in the flow of time through approximately 250 works encompassing Korean ancient art, modern and contemporary art, and international contemporary art.


This 《Yeoyeo Nature 如如自然》 exhibition proposes artistic practice that recovers 'natural as it is' nature and unmanipulated sensation based on the philosophy of 'wu wei (無爲)' derived from Taoist thought. By materializing the invisible concepts of 'breath', 'texture', and 'void' into four sensory spaces, visitors will be able to unfold a sensory journey of direct response and dwelling.


The exhibition brings together the breath of tradition and contemporary aesthetics on a single trajectory through works of various genres, including ceramics, painting, printmaking, ink painting, and poetry. 'Star One' contains the silence of ceramics centered on earth and fire, the molding of wu wei, while 'Star Two' traces the texture of emotion in repeated lines and resonance. 'Star Three' shows the temporal transition of sensation by placing ancient and contemporary art side by side, and 'Star Four' demonstrates how the void and silence become the language of thought.

name: Seoul Metropolitan Traditional Orchestra Chamber Music Series  - Sori Island: Arirang Through the Ages
summary: A Korean traditional chamber music concert commemorating the 80th anniversary of Liberation, this performance expresses the emotions of migration, solidarity, loss, and hope embedded in Arirang throug
description_html:
Arirang, the most iconic Korean folk song, embodies the soul of the Korean people. Passed down across time and borders, this song carries the memories of migration, solidarity, loss, and hope, and it is both the voice and emotional record of a nation.

Sori Island: Arirang Through the Ages is a chamber concert by the Seoul Metropolitan Traditional Orchestra, held in celebration of the 80th anniversary of Korea’s Liberation. This performance captures the breath of each era expressed through Arirang, delicately interpreted through the tones of traditional Korean instruments.

From the Imjin War and resistance militias to forced migrations, armed independence movements, and globalization, travel through modern Korean history following the melodies of Arirang.

This is a stage where Korea's history and emotions are conveyed not in words but in sound, through the rich, resonant timbre of traditional instruments. Highly recommended for those wishing to experience the depth of Korean traditional music.

name: Gesture Beyond the Canvas Exhibition
summary: 《Gesture Beyond the Canvas》 Exhibition runs until July 31st at Superior Gallery
description_html:
Superior Gallery has curated the exhibition 《Gesture Beyond the Canvas》 for July 2025. This exhibition demonstrates how brushstrokes, the fundamental element of painting, can function as a creative language with the power to lead artistic innovation, rather than merely being simple techniques or traces. The 《Gesture Beyond the Canvas》 exhibition focuses on the experimental spirit and creative acts of three artists who break away from the conventional framework, where traditional brushstrokes remain confined to reproduction, and attempt new expressions and reinterpret nature. Artists Kwon Jae-na, Lee Chae, and Choi Je-i each convey their artistic philosophy through their works, employing different perspectives and original brushwork.

In the 《Gesture Beyond the Canvas》 exhibition, we can see how the brushstrokes of these three artists do not simply remain within the canvas but extend to nature, life, and inner emotions. We anticipate that this exhibition will open new horizons in art, where the original brushwork and artistic challenges of artists Kwon Jae-na, Lee Chae, and Choi Je-i transcend the traditional painting framework, presenting new perspectives and sensations.

name: Veil Undrawn
summary: An exhibition illuminating the perspectives of three Korean female artists born in the 1990s, who navigate our digital age where the indiscriminate consumption of social media images exists alongside
description_html:
"Veil Undrawn" explores the contradictions of contemporary psychology and the delicate boundaries between surface and depth, as seen through the eyes of three Korean female artists born in the 1990s who navigate our digital age—an era where we consume social media images indiscriminately while simultaneously witnessing their infinite potential for expansion.

"Veil Undrawn" illuminates the thoughts and emotions of our time: the psychological contradictions of modern life—material abundance paired with spiritual emptiness, the belonging we find through social media alongside the isolation it creates—and examines how the AI-digital generation consumes imagery in entirely new ways, all filtered through the distinctive perspectives of these 1990s-born artists.
description_text: "Veil Undrawn" explores the contradictions of contemporary psychology and the delicate boundaries between surface and depth, as seen through the eyes of three Korean female artists born in the 1990s who navigate our digital age—an era where we consume social media images indiscriminately while simultaneously witnessing their infinite potential for expansion. "Veil Undrawn" illuminates the thoughts and emotions of our time: the psychological contradictions of modern life—material abundance paired with spiritual emptiness, the belonging we find through social media alongside the isolation it creates—and examines how the AI-digital generation consumes imagery in entirely new ways, all filtered through the distinctive perspectives of these 1990s-born artists.

name: Seonyudo: Silent Coexistence
summary: An exhibition designed to reflect the temporality and spatiality of Seonyudo Park, allowing visitors to freely walk through the space, engage with plants, and experience the flow of change
description_html: Seonyudo Park was once a water purification plant and industrial site, but it has since been transformed into an ecological sanctuary within the city. It is also a living ecosystem where various naturalized plants grow. Naturalized plants are non-native species that have adapted to new environments and now grow independently, quietly leaving traces of life in the ecology and landscape of Seoul. Artist Nahyun focuses on the life stories of migration, settlement, boundaries, and identity of these naturalized plants. In her exhibition Seonyudo: Silent Coexistence, she invites visitors to engage with plants and experience the ongoing flow of transformation.
description_text: Seonyudo Park was once a water purification plant and industrial site, but it has since been transformed into an ecological sanctuary within the city. It is also a living ecosystem where various naturalized plants grow. Naturalized plants are non-native species that have adapted to new environments and now grow independently, quietly leaving traces of life in the ecology and landscape of Seoul. Artist Nahyun focuses on the life stories of migration, settlement, boundaries, and identity of these naturalized plants. In her exhibition Seonyudo: Silent Coexistence, she invites visitors to engage with plants and experience the ongoing flow of transformation.

name: Christian Hidaka: Theatres of the Sky, Skies of the Theatre
summary: An exhibition featuring Japanese-British artist Christian Hidaka, offering a unique and intriguing experience through the fusion of Eastern and Western painting histories and techniques
description_html: Japanese-British artist Christian Hidaka presents a compelling experience by blending the painting traditions and techniques of East and West. Based on his unique perspective, the exhibition introduces a new visual language that bridges cultural and geographical heritages, creating a vivid and immersive painterly composition. The exhibition includes large-scale murals and showcases Hidaka’s distinctive experiments in painting, rarely seen until now. Notably, the artist integrates Western linear perspective and Eastern three-distance perspective, as well as Renaissance tempera and traditional Asian pigments like seokcheong, all made from natural materials. Through this harmony of East and West, nature and art are brought together on a single canvas. This exhibition aims not only to explore a practical approach to painting for the next generation but also to offer a moment to rediscover our presence and perception of the world. By stepping beyond the square boundaries of a canvas into a nonlinear chronology of imagination, visitors are invited to open the door to a visionary world reminiscent of ancient cave murals.
description_text: Japanese-British artist Christian Hidaka presents a compelling experience by blending the painting traditions and techniques of East and West. Based on his unique perspective, the exhibition introduces a new visual language that bridges cultural and geographical heritages, creating a vivid and immersive painterly composition. The exhibition includes large-scale murals and showcases Hidaka’s distinctive experiments in painting, rarely seen until now. Notably, the artist integrates Western linear perspective and Eastern three-distance perspective, as well as Renaissance tempera and traditional Asian pigments like seokcheong, all made from natural materials. Through this harmony of East and West, nature and art are brought together on a single canvas. This exhibition aims not only to explore a practical approach to painting for the next generation but also to offer a moment to rediscover our presence and perception of the world. By stepping beyond the square boundaries of a canvas into a nonlinear chronology of imagination, visitors are invited to open the door to a visionary world reminiscent of ancient cave murals.

name: 2025 SPO RIVERSIDE CONCERT
summary: A RIVERSIDE CONCERT at Yeouido Hangang Park conducted by Seoul Philharmonic's music director Jaap van Zweden
description_html:
The Seoul Philharmonic Orchestra will hold the "2025 Seoul Philharmonic Riverside Concert in Collaboration with the Federation of Korean Industries." Under the baton of Jaap van Zweden, the orchestra’s third music director and a Dutch conductor, the performance will take place against the romantic backdrop of the Han River on a summer night. The concert will feature orchestral music as well as collaborations with cello, trumpet, soprano, and baritone soloists. The performance will culminate in a spectacular fireworks display illuminating the early summer night sky, accompanied by beautiful classical melodies. This event is part of the "80th Anniversary of Liberation Commemoration Project" and is sponsored by the Federation of Korean Industries, which has led efforts to promote free market economy, sound economic development, and globalization.


The riverside concert is free and open to all citizens without prior registration. Entry to the 2,000-seat venue at Hangang Park will be on a first-come, first-served basis. Audience members may also enjoy the music freely around the venue using their own mats and portable chairs. Convenient access to the concert site is available via Subway Line 5, Yeouinaru Station. For those unable to attend in person, the concert will also be livestreamed on the Seoul Philharmonic Orchestra’s and Seoul City’s “Live Seoul” YouTube channels.

name: The Day and Night of Cheonggyecheon
summary: Special exhibition commemorating the 20th anniversary of the Cheonggyecheon Museum
description_html:

Though it was an era of great scarcity, Kim once said, “Even under the moonlight, there was romance in the humble shacks.”

Through these works, we hope visitors will encounter the radiant moments of those who lived difficult yet heartfelt lives.

name: Take My Eyes Off
summary: An exhibition that explores the practical potential of painting by showcasing contemporary works that seek a new kind of “visuality,” moving beyond conventional image environments and traditional line
description_html:
"Take my eyes off' focuses on contemporary painting caught in a complex and passionate entanglement with “vision” and “images.” This exhibition examines the strategies employed by today’s painters who, in response to an overwhelming visual landscape saturated with images, attempt to break free and search for a new visual language.

Using “eyes” as a central metaphor, the exhibition presents contemporary paintings that challenge established modes of seeing, thus revealing painting’s potential as a practice of resistance and renewal. 'Take my eyes off' invites viewers to encounter works that strive to “pull our eyes away” from today's image overload, offering insight into the story of painting as it confronts its own limitations."

name: Bonds of the Heart, Waves of Resonance
summary: The largest-scale exhibition in 40 years since 1985, revisiting the legacy of peace diplomacy and cultural exchange between Korea and Japan.
description_html:
This landmark exhibition celebrates 60 years of normalized diplomatic relations between Korea and Japan and the 80th anniversary of Korea’s liberation. It serves as a meaningful moment to reflect on the Korea-Japan relationship. While Japan remains Korea’s closest neighbor, many unresolved issues still hinder deeper cooperation. The more we reflect on the past and examine the present, the better we can prepare for a new turning point.


'Bonds of the Heart, Waves of Resonance' explores the essence of trust and exchange—between nations and between individuals—through the story of the Tongsinsa, the diplomatic missions of the Joseon Dynasty. While Tongsinsa refers to formal diplomatic delegations and systems, their deeper significance goes beyond diplomacy and cultural exchange. These missions were based on mutual respect, trust, and understanding, fostering friendship between nations and bonds between people.


History is not merely a record of the past—it is a force that connects the present and future. Through this historical legacy of Tongsinsa, which bridges state and individual, diplomacy and culture, past and present, this exhibition reflects on the meaning of "diplomacy based on trust" and encourages us to envision a peaceful future together.
description_text: This landmark exhibition celebrates 60 years of normalized diplomatic relations between Korea and Japan and the 80th anniversary of Korea’s liberation. It serves as a meaningful moment to reflect on the Korea-Japan relationship. While Japan remains Korea’s closest neighbor, many unresolved issues still hinder deeper cooperation. The more we reflect on the past and examine the present, the better we can prepare for a new turning point. 'Bonds of the Heart, Waves of Resonance' explores the essence of trust and exchange—between nations and between individuals—through the story of the Tongsinsa, the diplomatic missions of the Joseon Dynasty. While Tongsinsa refers to formal diplomatic delegations and systems, their deeper significance goes beyond diplomacy and cultural exchange. These missions were based on mutual respect, trust, and understanding, fostering friendship between nations and bonds between people. History is not merely a record of the past—it is a force that connects the present and future. Through this historical legacy of Tongsinsa, which bridges state and individual, diplomacy and culture, past and present, this exhibition reflects on the meaning of "diplomacy based on trust" and encourages us to envision a peaceful future together.

name: World Heritage and Capital Fortifications of Hanyang
summary: A special exhibition exploring the international value of Hanyang's capital fortifications
description_html:
2025 Seoul City Wall Museum First Half Special Exhibition


World Heritage and Capital Fortifications of Hanyang


The "Capital Fortifications of Hanyang" were built to defend Hanyang, the capital of Joseon. While many fortresses of historical heritage in many contemporary cities have disappeared due to urban development, Hanyang's capital fortifications have maintained their form to the present day, preserving both tangible and intangible historical value. To promote and conserve these values worldwide, Seoul City, Gyeonggi Province, Goyang City, and the National Heritage Administration are collaborating to inscribe Hanyang's capital fortifications on the World Heritage List.


This exhibition examines the meaning of UNESCO World Heritage, the World Heritage Convention and its operating bodies, the World Heritage inscription process, and the international value of Hanyang's capital fortifications, aiming to explore how Hanyang's capital fortifications are progressing from being solely Korea's heritage to becoming heritage for the entire world.
description_text: 2025 Seoul City Wall Museum First Half Special Exhibition World Heritage and Capital Fortifications of Hanyang The "Capital Fortifications of Hanyang" were built to defend Hanyang, the capital of Joseon. While many fortresses of historical heritage in many contemporary cities have disappeared due to urban development, Hanyang's capital fortifications have maintained their form to the present day, preserving both tangible and intangible historical value. To promote and conserve these values worldwide, Seoul City, Gyeonggi Province, Goyang City, and the National Heritage Administration are collaborating to inscribe Hanyang's capital fortifications on the World Heritage List. This exhibition examines the meaning of UNESCO World Heritage, the World Heritage Convention and its operating bodies, the World Heritage inscription process, and the international value of Hanyang's capital fortifications, aiming to explore how Hanyang's capital fortifications are progressing from being solely Korea's heritage to becoming heritage for the entire world.

name: Special Exhibition for the 80th Anniversary of Liberation "Prologue: With a Heart Singing to the Stars" from the Gana Art Collection
summary: A special exhibition from the Gana Art Collection reflecting Korea's social realities of the 1980s-90s, commemorating the 80th anniversary of liberation
description_html:
Seoul Museum of Art has organized a special exhibition from the Gana Art Collection to commemorate the 80th anniversary of Korea's liberation. The Gana Art Collection consists of 200 artworks donated to the Seoul Museum of Art in 2001 by Lee Ho-jae, representative of Gana Art, encompassing minjung art and realism works that actively reflected the 1980s-90s Korean social realities.


Eighty years after liberation, generations who directly experienced Japanese colonial rule, liberation, the Korean War, and the division of North and South Korea have been succeeded by generations who did not experience these events. Currently, 95% of South Korea's population was born after liberation, and they have learned about modern Korean history through historical records. This exhibition aims to provide an opportunity for more profound empathy with the era by examining social, political, and historical contexts and personal narratives that were not highlighted in the grand narrative of modern Korean history through artistic works.


The exhibition is organized into four parts. The first part examines the history of hardship and sacrifice during Japanese colonial rule and the independence movement. The second part addresses the devastation of the Korean War and the tragedy of fratricidal conflict. The third part reflects on the tragedy and socio-political issues caused by the continued division after the war. The final part explores possibilities for the future through works depicting peaceful coexistence beyond war and conflict.


This exhibition particularly incorporates poetry from the 1940s-50s that conveys resistance and the will to overcome reality alongside the artworks, vividly delivering the resonance of the era. The poems contain earnest wishes for liberation, the cruelty of war overshadowed by death, and sorrow over the reality of North and South divided by ideological opposition, allowing visitors to indirectly experience that era when people persevered despite adversity.


The freedom we enjoy today is indebted to the sacrifices of previous generations. The freedom achieved through their dedication and courage is a precious heritage we must pass on to future generations. Through this exhibition commemorating the 80th anniversary of liberation, we hope to reflect on the value of liberation and create a prologue opening to a future of peace and reconciliation.

description_html: Space K Seoul is pleased to present 《Dreams for Hire》, a solo exhibition by London-based artist Minyoung Choi (b.1989). The artist gathers fragments of memories from her childhood and experiences of migration and presents them as dreamlike scenes between dreams and reality. Dolphins appear in the Han River at sunset, penguins appear next to a person asleep in the living room, or a rainbow in the middle of the night shines like a cluster of moons, creating a new landscape where elements that wouldn't coexist on the same screen are mixed together. The artist's magical realist landscapes invite us to imagine unique narratives and meanings. Minyoung Choi's strange and familiar world feels like dreams where the impossible is realized, and they allow us to look at the various realities we encounter in a new light.

name: Empty Houses on the Coast
summary: This is an exhibition of paintings by Korean artists that explores various aspects of empty houses.
description_html:
The artist’s paintings ‘A series of empty houses’ are deep multidimensional structures containing improbable transpositions of time and space. She re-assembles the fragments of memory that she has gathered from the shoreline. We are drawn in to the structures and we find ourselves surrounded by floors made of ice, windows through which we can see a raging sea by moonlight and where, the sea itself is advancing in to the room and we are really standing on a beach. Viewrs could be active participants in a multi-faceted space where gravity has been suspended.
Film stories are fiction, but when those single frames are assembled and viewed together they create the powerful illusion of having witnessed an 'event', no matter how unlikely that event might be. 'Empty Houses on the Coast' leaves me with exactly that sensation of having witnessed the improbable come to life.

name: Souimun, the Lost Gate of Seoul City Wall
summary: 2024 Seoul City Wall Museum Second Half-Year Special Exhibition: Souimun, the Lost Gate of the Seoul City Wall
description_html: Souimun Gate was a gate of the Hanyangdoseong (the Seoul City Wall), located between Sungnyemun Gate and Donuimun Gate, serving as the southwestern passage of Hanyang during the Joseon Dynasty. The area around Souimun Gate was a bustling hub of land and water transportation, filled with goods and people from all over the country. Outside the gate, executions of serious criminals and Catholic believers who were thought to threaten Confucian ideology were carried out, making it widely known that severe punishments awaited those who committed crimes. During the Japanese occupation, Souimun Gate was demolished in 1914 for road improvements, as it was perceived as an obstacle to urban modernization. This exhibition provides an opportunity to explore the bustling scenes and the history of demolition of Souimun Gate, which guarded the southwestern part of the Seoul City Wall.

description_html:
Do you have something that represents you? For artist Lee Dong-hoon, Bruno serves that role. Bruno stands as a representative of the artist and a protagonist in the world he wishes to express. In this exhibition, Bruno is depicted as more peaceful and safe than ever before. We encapsulate this peace and safety with the word ‘rest.’ In response to the question 'What is rest?', author Lee Ki-joo describes it as 'a time to gather energy in life' in his book <Universal Words>. Nowadays, everyone prides themselves on living a busy life. "However, isn’t living without true rest like ignoring the low battery warning on your phone, knowing it will soon run out, and feeling anxious?" Through his paintings, the artist seeks to remind us of the importance of rest in our lives. Moreover, he emphasizes the need for purity, sincerity, and even childhood innocence as human beings. Through depictions of daily life or stories of rest, the artist aims to convey happiness, peace, and comfort of the mind using the medium of painting. Did you find yourself in the image of Bruno in the artwork? If so, you are already someone who fully relaxes your mind. If not, then we can find it together right now. We hope your hearts find complete rest at Samseyoung Galary.

Bruno stands as a representative of the artist and a protagonist in the world he wishes to express. In this exhibition, Bruno is depicted as more peaceful and safe than ever before. We encapsulate this peace and safety with the word ‘rest.’ In response to the question 'What is rest?', author Lee Ki-joo describes it as 'a time to gather energy in life' in his book <Universal Words>. Nowadays, everyone prides themselves on living a busy life. "However, isn’t living without true rest like ignoring the low battery warning on your phone, knowing it will soon run out, and feeling anxious?" Through his paintings, the artist seeks to remind us of the importance of rest in our lives. Moreover, he emphasizes the need for purity, sincerity, and even childhood innocence as human beings. Through depictions of daily life or stories of rest, the artist aims to convey happiness, peace, and comfort of the mind using the medium of painting. Did you find yourself in the image of Bruno in the artwork? If so, you are already someone who fully relaxes your mind. If not, then we can find it together right now. We hope your hearts find complete rest at Samseyoung Galary. Curator Shim Da-seul

name: Yoo Eui Jeong 《The Baek-Ja 》
summary: Gallery Jiwooheon will present a solo exhibition, "The Baek-Ja (The White Porcelain)," by Yoo Eui-Jeong, one of Korea's leading ceramic artists, from November 13 to December 21.
description_html:
Ceramic art, considered one of humanity's oldest forms of expression, embodies the symbolic language and imaginative structures refined through history. 

As the artist notes, ceramics have reflected their time's philosophy, aesthetics, lifestyles, and trends through color, shape, and pattern. Yoo Eui-jeong focuses on this inherent nature of ceramics, creating works with a hybrid temporality.

One of Yoo's signature techniques involves allowing glaze to drip over white porcelain and layering it with iconic imagery from both the past and present. The way the glaze's form fades and distorts as it flows downward symbolizes the evolving cultural symbols shaped by the passage of time.

In this exhibition, Yoo Eui-jeong draws inspiration from Baekja, which reached its zenith during the Joseon Dynasty, presenting works that reflect contemporary relevance. White porcelain, originally a symbol of the royal court's dignity, also became widely cherished by commoners for its simplicity, with blue-and-white porcelain and iron-painted porcelain dominating different social strata. Yoo experiments with how baekja, imbued with such historical context, can manifest in meaningful ways from a modern perspective.

name: The Persistence of Self
summary: Special Exhibition of Kim Young-sik, Master Potter and Intangible Cultural Heritage of Gyeongsangbuk-do and Joseon Kiln Mun Mountain
description_html:
The story of Kim Young-sik, a master potter recognized as an intangible cultural heritage of Gyeongsangbuk-do, traces back to the Joseon Dynasty. According to Hajae Diary, written by Ji Kyushik, an official supplier of various wares to the royal court and government offices, Kim’s great-grandfather, Kim Bi-an, constructed a Mangdaengi kiln in 1903, confirming Kim’s lineage as a descendant of royal porcelain artisans. For nearly 300 years, the family has upheld the tradition of Joseon white porcelain, and Kim Young-sik, as the eighth-generation master, brings a unique artistic "persistence" to his craft.
The “Persistence of Self” exhibition showcases Kim’s dedication to the tradition of Joseon white porcelain. Through his resolute commitment, he creates hard and beautiful porcelain fired at high temperatures. This exhibition highlights his blue-and-white porcelain's purity and understated elegance, born from his unwavering craftsmanship. Bonsai plants, radiating a vibrant energy, are also displayed to enhance his artistic vision. The exhibition celebrates the depth and value of Korean cultural heritage, sustained through one man’s determination and dedication.

name: Marriage Stories of Seoul Families
summary: The exhibition “Marriage Stories of Seoul Families” introduces the marriage culture of Seoul residents.
description_html: Marriage, once seen solely as a duty, is now considered a choice. To examine the pivotal moments behind these changes, the Seoul Urban Life Museum conducted an era-by-era study of the marriage culture of Seoul residents last year, culminating in this year's special exhibition. Although Korean society faced the Korean War following the 1945 liberation, it rapidly advanced, achieving the Miracle on the Hangang River, which significantly impacted marriage culture. The marriage culture of Seoul, shaped by a blend of tradition and foreign influences, continues to evolve today. We hope that looking back on the 80-year transformation of Seoul residents' marriage culture since liberation will encourage reflection on our society’s journey and foster greater generational understanding.

name: Someday, we will be in the same.
summary: One day, from our unique paths, may we come together in a shared sense of healing.
description_html:
Artist Choi Jae-Yi continues her work under the belief that the deeply personal is also universal. After enduring a period of illness, she found inspiration in the sight of trees lying exposed to the sea breeze in Jeju, using this as a motif in her work. She began to express the contrast between wind and home—where wind represents abstraction and freedom, and home serves as a final point of emotional expression. Through her work, she engages in an internal dialogue, finding both emotional liberation and healing in the act of creation. 

On the other hand, artist Hwang Ho-Seok jots down striking words or ideas for his work. He reflects on them over time, creating stories and images, often choosing photos he has previously taken. He then discovers and expresses unnoticed details or emotions within these photos. He seeks to translate intimate feelings drawn from everyday life and relationships into his paintings, hoping viewers will find healing through this expression. 

Through Roland Barthes' concept of nuance, the works of these two artists encompass more than mere differences; they depict emotions in distinct ways, allowing for varied interpretations. This divergence shapes the mood of each piece, offering viewers a more profound emotional connection. Despite their contrasting motifs and approaches, both artists share a common purpose: to explore emotional healing. They invite viewers to freely interpret and find solace in their works, subtly whispering that each person can find personal healing within the relationship between their everyday lives and surroundings. 

– Curator Sim Da-Seul

name: Seoul Archives Children’s Record Experience Room <Twisting Record Exploration>
summary: A play-based experiential exhibition aimed at children aged 7 to 13 to easily understand records
description_html: The Seoul Archives has prepared an interactive exhibition for children, “The Twisting Record Exploration”, designed to help them easily and enjoyably experience records. The exhibition is divided into three main sections. Part 1, “From Memory to Record”, allows visitors to explore various methods of remembering, learn about recording tools, and understand different types of records. Part 2, “Record Exploration”, features an interactive experience where participants can examine records of Seoul and their records and even build landmarks based on the records held by the Seoul Archives. Part 3, “The Record Keepers”, introduces the roles of record researchers and preservation scientists who collect and preserve records. As a specialized public archive, the Seoul Archives not only collects and preserves Seoul's records and residents' memories but also strives to provide diverse record information services. We hope this children’s interactive exhibition will inspire more citizens to take an interest in records and actively participate in the documentation world.

name: Seoul Mini Mountains
summary: The Seoul Museum of History presents the exhibition <Seoul Mini Mountains>: Reading the City from its Voids!
description_html:
The “Seoul Mini Mountains” exhibition is rooted in a research project by Borio-Lab, led by Géraldine Borio, an assistant professor at the University of Hong Kong’s Department of Architecture. With over 17 years of architectural and urban research experience across Asian cities such as Bangkok, Hong Kong, and Seoul, Professor Borio’s work forms the foundation of this exhibition.
Jointly presented with the Seoul Museum of History, the exhibition revisits Seoul’s urban landscape by investigating the role and impact of voids (empty spaces) in the city center on its urban narrative and identity. The exhibition highlights Seoul's distinctive topography through photographs and drawings created by Professor Borio and her students.
This research delves into how historical developments have shaped the voids in Seoul and how their ‘boundaries’ have changed. It analyzes these spaces through the observation of the ‘activities’ occurring within these undeveloped areas. You are invited to take part in this meaningful opportunity to experience a foreign scholar’s fresh perspective on Seoul and to reflect on the value of seeing spaces and objects in a new light. We look forward to your visit.

name: My Treasures, My Heritage
summary: A Museum Created by Citizens
description_html:
The museum is a place where memories are preserved and shared. The Seoul Museum of History actively encourages citizen donations to collect materials that embody Seoul’s history and culture and introduces newly donated items through exhibitions.

This year, they have prepared a special exhibition focusing on items donated from 25 different places last year. Although each piece varies in the time it holds and its rarity, every item is a precious treasure to both the donors and the museum.

To better highlight the value of these materials, the museum restores items in poor condition, translates classical Chinese texts into modern Korean for better understanding, and creates a more visitor-friendly exhibition environment.

As you explore the exhibition, they hope you enjoy the time spent sharing these diverse treasures and memories.

name: 2024 Seongbuk Newspaper Persona Project: 'Lee Tae-jun: It Seemed Even the Moonlight Was Regrettable to Him' Exhibition
summary: The "Newspaper Persona Project" aims to reinterpret the works and lives of modern and contemporary writers from Seongbuk through the diverse perspectives of today's artists.
description_html: Lee Tae-jun is recognized as an outstanding novelist in Korean literary history, but he also embodied various personas beyond literature. In the 1930s and 1940s, he was the editor of the prominent literary magazine Munjang, an antique enthusiast, the head of the cultural affairs department at a newspaper, a museum curator, and an art critic. Five creators—Kwon Hye-won (visual arts), Kim Seon-joo (architect), Kim Won-jin (visual arts), Park Sun-min (visual arts), and Layers Lab (book curation)—have brought Lee Tae-jun into the present-day. They immersed themselves in his life and literary works through a preliminary reading session. After more than six months of processing, they each transformed their experiences into creative works. This event is expected to create a space where literature and other forms of art can naturally meet across time, much like how Lee Tae-jun traversed the boundaries of art in the 1930s.

name: Jo Yongjin · Hwang Taein <A Gentle Change>
summary: A Gentle Change is a performance by Jo Yongjin and Hwang Taein, who have been active with the National Dance Company of Korea for over ten years.
description_html: A Gentle Change begins by asking whether Korean dance can offer something new to contemporary audiences. Jo Yongjin and Hwang Taein, who have been part of the National Dance Company of Korea for over ten years, aim to present "Korean dance" as a free and open expression unbound by fixed frameworks or limitations. They view Korean dance not as something owned by anyone or tied to a specific origin but as a living art form with the potential for continuous growth and expansion. They focus on finding a contemporary sensibility through a fresh perspective. By showcasing various interpretations of this long-preserved art form, they seek to draw out the dance's inherently captivating elements. At the same time, they explore the idea that Korean dance is not merely an ancient cultural heritage but a living art form with the potential for continuous growth and expansion.

name: SeMA Omnibus : At the End of the World Split Endlessly
summary: This exhibition interprets the Seoul Museum of Art's collection through the keywords of connection and combination between mediums. It explores the essential structure between artists and their works
description_html:
At the End of the World Splits Endlessly seeks to interpret SeMA’s collection through the keywords of connection and combination between mediums. In this post-medium/post-media era, the exhibition explores the inevitable structure between artists and their works, mediated by technology, while showcasing the multi-layered structure of media today. It examines how old and new media, virtual and real, AI and the body, and the interplay of technology and society create complex media environments. The term "medium" originates from the Greek word for "middle" or "between," signifying how, in contemporary art, mediums function as a bridge—linking the artist, the artwork, the viewer, and the museum. As visitors follow the exhibition's key concepts—Old & New, Yellow Block, Layered Medium, Open End—it reveals our current media landscape's singular and plural structures.

Inspired by anthropologist Anna Tsing’s The Mushroom at the End of the World and Jorge Luis Borges’ The Garden of Forking Paths, this exhibition grapples with the questions posed by the climate crisis and the end of capitalism. Through their works, artists ask where we stand in the world as it fractures. Just as artists traverse a spectrum of media, choosing and renewing their mediums, we, too, dream of new connections in a world that endlessly diverges. These connections, however, are not seamless but fragmented and partial. Art encourages us to confront this imperfection, urging us to find life, reflection, resistance, hope, and imagination among the ruins and potentialities of our time.

name: Lee Youngjun Ingoing Escape
summary: Gallery Jiwoohon will hold Lee Young-jun's solo exhibition <Ingoing Escape> from September 4th to October 12th.
description_html: Lee Youngjun's solo exhibition “Ingoing Escape” is organized to coincide with the Kiaf and Frieze seasons to introduce noteworthy emerging artists. It is also part of the 2024 Seoul Art Week. Based in Munich, Germany, Lee Youngjun has been expanding his activities in Korea since last year. He is an experimental artist who reinterprets space and form, drawing on personal narratives and emotions. The exhibition's theme, “Ingoing Escape,” means “escape inward,” emphasizing the artist's distinctive multidimensional abstraction. Lee Youngjun's works are created using a technique of layering various materials on canvas, with each layer maintaining its unique form without blending, effectively showcasing the dimensionality of time. Through this exhibition, viewers will experience a paradoxical encounter, simultaneously delving into their consciousness and confronting the multi-layered aspects of perception.

This exhibition reflects our hopes for the union of nature and industrial society, striving for natural harmony. We hope you enjoy a unique reflective experience through the works of these two artists, displayed in the traditional Hanok setting.

Visitors are invited to a journey to the solar system's ninth planet, a world filled with new possibilities.

name: CHUN Kyung-ja Centennial 《Turbulent Times: Women Life Art》
summary: Celebrating the 100th anniversary of Chun Kyung-ja's birth (1924–2015)
description_html: The Seoul Museum of Art will host the exhibition “Turbulent Times: Women Life Art” in 2024 to commemorate the 100th anniversary of Chun Kyung-ja’s birth (1924–2015). This exhibition will feature works and archives from 22 female artists who lived during the same period as Chun Kyung-ja. Unlike previous exhibitions or research, this exhibition highlights Chun Kyung-ja’s modern mindset and influence on her era. It also sheds light on other female artists of her time who, unlike Chun, struggled to break free from the traditional confines of Eastern painting during the Japanese occupation. These women collectively lived through a tumultuous era marked by significant historical events, including the Japanese colonial era (1909–1945), Korea’s liberation on August 15, 1945, the Korean War (1950–1953), the April 19 Revolution (1960), the May 16 military coup (1961), military dictatorship (1961–1979), the December 12 military rebellion (1979), the May 18 Gwangju Democratization Movement (1980), the new military regime (1980–1993), and the ongoing democratization movements following the establishment of the South Korean government. Society, personal life, and art are inseparable, and this exhibition aims to explore the interconnectedness of political, social, and artistic trends from the Japanese colonial period to the 1990s. By examining the broader context of the Eastern art scene during that time, it seeks to reveal the influence of these movements on the artists. The exhibition will cover various aspects, including educational institutions during the colonial period, the development of the Joseon Art Exhibition (Chosun Misun), post-liberation educational institutions, and the National Art Exhibition (Gukjeon), along with the political and social interventions that occurred in between. It will also provide a detailed and objective look at the trajectory of Eastern painting, group activities, achievements, and individual biographies of the artists. This approach helps to better understand their artistic worlds and trace their evolution from being labeled as "female Eastern painters" to becoming the "artists" they are recognized today. This exhibition delves deeply into various materials, including Chun Ja's candid autobiography, various articles, writings, and artworks. By thoroughly researching these sources, the exhibition aims to uncover the many individuals who played a role in her life and explore her relationships with them. A carefully organized biography will correct past misunderstandings and inaccuracies about the artist, paving the way for more in-depth research in the future. Through this exhibition, we honor Chun Kyung-ja, a pioneer of modern Korean art, while shedding light on the works of other artists who lived through the "era of turbulence" and contributed to the development of modern Korean art with their diverse creations. The exhibition reexamines the artistic worlds of Chung Chan-young, Lee Hyun-ok, Chung Yong-hee, Bae Jeong-rye, Park Rae-hyun, Chun Kyung-ja, Park In-kyung, Geum Dong-won, Moon Eun-hee, Lee In-sil, Lee Kyung-ja, Jang Sang-eui, Ryu Min-ja, Lee Sook-ja, Oh Nang-ja, Yoon Ae-geun, Lee Hwa-ja, Shim Kyung-ja, Won Moon-ja, Song Su-ryeon, Joo Min-sook, Kim Choon-ok, and Cha Myung-hee, without boundaries or limitations, within the context of contemporary art movements.
